title: Kindergarten daily reading
overview: One hundred eighty nights of adult-read poetry, stories, and nature writing invite children to listen, wonder, retell, and notice language. Every ten-minute session includes conversation; short poems invite rereading, gesture, or drawing, and longer stories continue over consecutive nights with a short recap. All print is supplied by the adult, and oral or nonverbal responses are welcome. The sequence grows from hearing patterns and naming details toward connecting events and supporting interpretations, without assuming that beginning readers can decode these literary texts.

progression.focus: Hear patterns, picture a scene, and recall an event.
progression.rationale: Adults read every text. Children can speak, point, move, or draw while familiar scenes, repeated sounds, short story sequences, and concrete nature observations make listening participation possible.

progression.focus: Follow changes and compare two details.
progression.rationale: Listeners connect beginnings and endings, track simple causes, and hear how sound and image contribute to a poem or short narrative.

progression.focus: Distinguish make-believe, observation, and a speaker’s view.
progression.rationale: Listeners compare nature observations with imagined scenes and distinguish what a character believes from what a narrator shows. Adult support helps them separate an observed detail from an explanation and support a choice with a phrase.

progression.focus: Hold several events or images in mind.
progression.rationale: More developed stories and poems invite retelling, prediction checked against the ending, and comparison of characters’ choices.

progression.focus: Explain a change using details from across a text.
progression.rationale: Children connect a problem to its resolution and use concrete language to explain shifts in feeling, setting, or perspective; rereading remains available.

progression.focus: Offer and support a personal interpretation.
progression.rationale: Children increasingly choose the words or moments that support an idea, while adults still supply all print reading and vocabulary support. The course does not assume independent decoding.

days.title: The Swing
days.challenge: Hear a changing view while following the swing’s up-and-down movement.
days.focus: A repeated movement organizes the speaker’s joy.
days.context: Read once, then let the child trace the swing’s rise and fall with a hand.

excerpt.locator:
The Swing; begins “HOW do you like to go up in a swing,
Up in the air so blue?”; ends “Up in the air I go flying again,
Up in the air and down!”.

questions.prompt: What can the child see over when the swing goes high?
facilitatorNotes: Listen for the wall, then accept any correctly named feature of the wider view.
evidence: Up in the air and over the wall,

questions.prompt: How does the view change when the child looks down?
facilitatorNotes: The broad countryside gives way to the garden and roof below. Pointing or drawing is enough.
evidence: Down on the roof so brown

questions.prompt: Which ending words can your hand move with?
facilitatorNotes: Invite an up-and-down gesture; the final words make the repeated movement audible.
evidence: Up in the air and down!

days.title: The Clock
days.challenge: Hear the shift from describing a clock to addressing people.
days.focus: A clock’s parts become an image for human behaviour.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE CLOCK”; opening “There's a neat little clock,--”; ending “To do what is right.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the little clock stand, and what do its hands do?
facilitatorNotes: It stands in the schoolroom and points to the time. Explain that clock hands point rather than grasp.
evidence: In the schoolroom it stands,

questions.prompt: What could it mean for both a clock and a child to have a clean, bright face?
facilitatorNotes: A clock has a face with its numbers; a person has a face too. Accept noticing the playful shared word.
evidence: Keep a face clean and bright,

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza ask us only to tell the time? What else does it ask?
facilitatorNotes: It wishes that our hands be ready to do right. Invite an example of helping, while keeping that example separate from the poem.
evidence:
With hands ever ready
  To do what is right.

days.title: Mix a pancake
days.challenge: Remember a short sequence of action words.
days.focus: Quick commands turn cooking into a playful rhyme.
days.context: Read aloud twice; mime the actions without cooking.

excerpt.locator:
Mix a pancake; begins “Mix a pancake,
Stir a pancake,”; ends “Toss the pancake,—
Catch it if you can.”.

questions.prompt: What happens before the pancake goes into the pan?
facilitatorNotes: Mixing and stirring come first; invite two gestures in order.
evidence:
Mix a pancake,
Stir a pancake,

questions.prompt: Which word tells us how the pancake is cooked?
facilitatorNotes: Fry names the cooking action. Explain it briefly if unfamiliar.
evidence: Fry the pancake,

questions.prompt: Why does the last line feel like a little challenge?
facilitatorNotes: Catching a tossed pancake might be difficult; the ending invites an imagined attempt.
evidence: Catch it if you can.

days.title: Two Bad Mice, part 1: an inviting tiny house
days.challenge: Notice clues that distinguish a toy meal from a real one.
days.focus: Detailed setting creates the mice’s mistaken expectation.
days.context: Two mice explore a doll’s house while its dolls are out. Muslin is a thin cloth, and a perambulator is a carriage for a baby or doll.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Two Bad Mice, paragraphs 1–12; begins “ONCE upon a time there was a very beautiful doll's-house; …” and ends “… and lead knives and forks, and two dolly-chairs--all _so_ convenient!”.

questions.prompt: Which details make the little house seem like a real home?
facilitatorNotes: Possible answers include curtains, a door, chimney, and dining room. Ask for a detail actually heard.
evidence: real muslin curtains and a front door and a chimney.

questions.prompt: What is strange about Jane being the cook?
facilitatorNotes: She never cooks; the pretend dinner was purchased already made. Discuss the difference between a doll’s job and a real person’s actions.
evidence: she never did any cooking

questions.prompt: Why are the mice so happy when they reach the dining room?
facilitatorNotes: They think they have found a lovely dinner and useful tiny furniture. The food’s refusal to leave the plates is a clue listeners can notice before the mice understand.
evidence: Then they squeaked with joy!

days.title: Two Bad Mice, part 2: the dinner will not move
days.challenge: Link repeated failed attempts with growing frustration.
days.focus: The food’s true material explains the earlier mystery.
days.context: The mice have entered a doll’s dining room and expect to eat the beautiful dinner. These objects are pretend food, though the mice do not yet understand.
days.contentNote: The mice break pretend food and throw doll clothing; discuss frustration without endorsing damage.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Two Bad Mice, paragraphs 13–27; begins “TOM THUMB set to work at once to carve the …” and ends “… and he threw them out of the top floor window.”.

questions.prompt: What explanation does Tom first give for the hard ham?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks it has not been boiled enough. This is his mistaken explanation, not the narrator’s final explanation.
evidence: It is not boiled enough; it is hard.

questions.prompt: What do the mice discover underneath the ham’s paint?
facilitatorNotes: It is plaster, not food. Let the child explain why more cooking would not solve the problem.
evidence: it was made of nothing but plaster!

questions.prompt: How do the noises bang, bang, smash, smash change the mood?
facilitatorNotes: They make the destruction sound loud and angry after the earlier quiet room. Accept sound imitation and an explanation of anger or disappointment.
evidence: bang, bang, smash, smash!

days.title: Two Bad Mice, part 3: carrying away and giving back
days.challenge: Track the change from taking objects to repairing harm.
days.focus: The ending complicates the title’s description of bad mice.
days.context: The angry mice have damaged the doll’s dinner. Hunca Munca now notices things useful for her own home. A bolster is a long pillow; a sixpence is an old coin.
days.contentNote: A mousetrap is proposed but no mouse is caught. The ending describes restitution after damage.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Two Bad Mice, paragraphs 28–41 (end); begins “But Hunca Munca had a frugal mind. After pulling half …” and ends “… her dust-pan and her broom to sweep the Dollies' house!”.

questions.prompt: Which stolen objects cannot fit into the mouse-hole?
facilitatorNotes: The book-case and bird-cage are too big. Ask the child to contrast them with something the mice do carry home.
evidence: The book-case and the bird-cage refused to go into the mouse-hole.

questions.prompt: How do the little girl and the nurse propose different ways to stop the mice?
facilitatorNotes: The girl wants a doll policeman; the nurse proposes a real trap. Their ideas differ because one belongs to pretend play and one could catch mice.
evidence: I will get a doll dressed like a policeman!

questions.prompt: What two actions at the end show an attempt to make things better?
facilitatorNotes: Tom pays with a found coin and Hunca Munca sweeps each morning. Discuss whether an apology or repair can matter after damage; different judgments are acceptable.
evidence: Hunca Munca comes with her dust-pan and her broom to sweep the Dollies' house!

days.title: Winter
days.challenge: Connect two details to the season named at the end.
days.focus: Wind and snow announce a season through physical sensations.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “WINTER”; opening “Cold and raw the north wind doth blow,”; ending “And winter's now come fairly.”.

questions.prompt: What has covered all the hills?
facilitatorNotes: Snow covers the hills. Invite a gesture showing a covering rather than requiring a drawing.
evidence: All the hills are covered with snow,

questions.prompt: Would this north wind feel warm or uncomfortable? Which words make you think so?
facilitatorNotes: Cold, raw and bleak support a chilly, uncomfortable feeling. Let the child echo the wind sounds softly.
evidence: Cold and raw the north wind doth blow,

questions.prompt: How does the speaker know winter has arrived before saying its name?
facilitatorNotes: The cold wind and snow are evidence within this scene. Note that winters differ by place; this is the poem’s particular setting.
evidence: And winter's now come fairly.

days.title: Learning to go alone
days.challenge: Follow a small journey from encouragement to arrival.
days.focus: The speaker’s caring voice supports a child’s first steps.
days.context: An adult is speaking to a young child learning to walk; the listener can move fingers as little feet.

excerpt.locator: Learning to go alone; begins “Come, my darling, come away,”; ends “After such a walk as this.”.

questions.prompt: What is the little child being invited to do?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker invites a walk; the small feet suggest a new walker.
evidence: Up and down with little feet,

questions.prompt: What help does the speaker offer near the end?
facilitatorNotes: The adult offers a finger to hold, a concrete sign of support.
evidence: Here’s my finger, hold it fast;

questions.prompt: Does this speaker sound cross or pleased? What words help you decide?
facilitatorNotes: Affectionate names and the kiss support pleased or loving; accept another feeling with evidence.
evidence: Now one pretty little kiss,

days.title: Dame Trot and Her Cat
days.challenge: Infer a relationship from the cat’s patient action.
days.focus: A peaceful household is shown through sharing a meal.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “DAME TROT AND HER CAT”; opening “Dame Trot and her cat”; ending “A nice piece from her plate.”.

questions.prompt: What does Pussy do while Dame Trot has dinner?
facilitatorNotes: The cat waits rather than taking the meal. Ask the child to show waiting quietly.
evidence: Pussy would wait,

questions.prompt: Why might Pussy be happy to wait beside the plate?
facilitatorNotes: The cat expects a nice piece of dinner. The text makes that reward certain, not merely possible.
evidence:
And was sure to receive
  A nice piece from her plate.

questions.prompt: What sometimes troubles their peaceful life: their meal or other people’s disagreements?
facilitatorNotes: Other folks’ strife interrupts peace. Explain strife as arguments; do not invent a quarrel between Dame and cat.
evidence:
When they were not troubled
  With other folks' strife.

days.title: Snow
days.challenge: Notice that the poem lets snowflakes answer a question.
days.focus: An imagined conversation changes falling snow into feathers and kisses.
days.context: The snow speaks in make-believe. Read the questions and answers in two gentle voices.

excerpt.locator: Snow; begins “LITTLE white feathers, filling the air--”; ends “But hold up your face, and we'll kiss you true."”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker call the bits of snow?
facilitatorNotes: White feathers is a picture for the snowflakes, not a claim that snow is made of feathers.
evidence: Little white feathers!

questions.prompt: Where do the snowflakes say they came from?
facilitatorNotes: They imagine cloud-birds shaking their wings in the sky.
evidence: They're shaking their white wings up in the sky.

questions.prompt: What might a snowflake’s “kiss” feel like?
facilitatorNotes: A cold light touch fits a snowflake landing on a face; ask the child to connect the word with that image.
evidence: But hold up your face, and we'll kiss you true.

days.title: Eyes and No Eyes: the walk to school
days.challenge: Build a mental route from a sequence of places.
days.focus: A familiar daily walk becomes a plan for careful observation.
days.context: In this historical British nature reader, three children describe what they notice outdoors. A common is shared open land; gorse is a flowering shrub. The children’s voices frame the author’s nature descriptions.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Introduction, printed pages 5–6, paragraphs 1–5 (end of lesson); begins “We three friends, Peter, Peggy, and Paul, walk to school …” and ends “… us all we see and put it in a book.”.

questions.prompt: What can Peter do well even though he is just learning to read?
facilitatorNotes: He notices things in the hedges. The passage values careful looking as well as reading.
evidence: But he has sharp eyes.

questions.prompt: Which places lie between the meeting pond and the school?
facilitatorNotes: The lane, common, wood, and fields. A child can draw or gesture along the route while the adult rereads it.
evidence: along a narrow lane, across the common, through the wood

questions.prompt: How will the observations become something the friends can keep?
facilitatorNotes: Paul will write them in a book. The final sentence explains why the narrator is collecting these details.
evidence: write down for us all we see and put it in a book.

days.title: Tweedle-dum and Tweedle-dee
days.challenge: Retell the cause of the quarrel and the event that interrupts it.
days.focus: A quarrel ends through an unexpected, oversized visitor.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: Two characters threaten a pretend battle, but no fight occurs; a large crow startles them.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “TWEEDLE-DUM AND TWEEDLE-DEE”; opening “Tweedle-dum and Tweedle-dee”; ending “They quite forgot their quarrel.”.

questions.prompt: What does Tweedle-dum say happened to his rattle?
facilitatorNotes: He says Tweedle-dee spoiled it. Keep the accusation distinct from proof that it happened.
evidence: Had spoiled his nice new rattle.

questions.prompt: How big does the poem make the crow sound?
facilitatorNotes: As big as a tar barrel: imagine a very large barrel beside the small rattle. Its exaggerated size creates surprise.
evidence: As big as a tar barrel,

questions.prompt: Do they settle their quarrel by fighting? What actually happens?
facilitatorNotes: They forget the quarrel when frightened by the crow. The poem never describes the threatened battle occurring.
evidence: They quite forgot their quarrel.

days.title: At the Sea-side
days.challenge: Connect digging with the water that follows.
days.focus: A small beach discovery is compressed into six lines.
days.context: A spade is a small digging shovel. Reread and trace a hole in the air.

excerpt.locator:
At the Sea-side; begins “WHEN I was down beside the sea
A wooden spade they gave to me”; ends “In every hole the sea came up,
Till it could come no more.”.

questions.prompt: What tool does the child have at the beach?
facilitatorNotes: A wooden spade is explicitly named.
evidence: A wooden spade they gave to me

questions.prompt: What happens in each hole the child digs?
facilitatorNotes: Sea water comes up into each hole.
evidence: In every hole the sea came up,

questions.prompt: Why might the child compare a hole to a cup?
facilitatorNotes: Both are hollow spaces that can hold water. A cupped hand can help picture the comparison.
evidence: My holes were empty like a cup,

days.title: Pat-a-Cake
days.challenge: Remember an action sequence and notice who will share the result.
days.focus: Rhythm accompanies the ordered actions of making a cake.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAT-A-CAKE”; opening “Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake,”; ending “For Tommy and me.”.

questions.prompt: What three actions happen before the cake goes into the oven?
facilitatorNotes: Pat it, prick it and mark it with T. Reread while miming with empty hands; no cooking materials are needed.
evidence:
Pat it, and prick it,
  And mark it with T,

questions.prompt: Which letter marks this cake, and whose name begins with that sound in the rhyme?
facilitatorNotes: T marks the cake and Tommy begins with T. This is an optional adult-supported sound connection, not a decoding demand.
evidence: For Tommy and me.

questions.prompt: How can you tell the baker is being asked to work quickly?
facilitatorNotes: The response says as fast as I can. Try a lively reading, keeping the words clear.
evidence: As fast as I can.

days.title: The Three Bears, part 1: three bowls of porridge
days.workTitle: The Story of the Three Bears
days.challenge: Hear a three-part pattern and notice the final variation.
days.focus: Repetition makes differences in size and temperature memorable.
days.context: Three bears leave their breakfast to cool, and a girl called Goldilocks enters their house without asking. Steel’s telling is read in three parts on three nights.
days.contentNote: The narrator repeatedly labels Goldilocks rude or badly brought up. Keep discussion on her choices and their effects rather than labeling children.

excerpt.locator: The Story of the Three Bears, 1922 edition pp. 19–20, paragraphs 1–3; begins “Once upon a time there were three Bears, who lived …” and ends “… so well, that she ate it all up, every bit!”.

questions.prompt: What belongings come in three different sizes?
facilitatorNotes: Bowls, chairs, and beds. The repeated list establishes a pattern listeners can anticipate.
evidence: a little bowl for the Little Wee Bear

questions.prompt: Why have the bears left the house?
facilitatorNotes: They are waiting for porridge to cool. Their absence is temporary, not an invitation to take breakfast.
evidence: while the porridge was cooling

questions.prompt: How is the third tasting different from the first two?
facilitatorNotes: It is just right, so she eats all the little bear’s porridge. The final event both completes and changes the pattern.
evidence: she ate it all up, every bit!

days.title: The Three Bears, part 2: a pattern leaves clues
days.workTitle: The Story of the Three Bears
days.challenge: Remember Goldilocks’s actions as the owners discover their effects.
days.focus: The repeated pattern returns from a new point of view.
days.context: Goldilocks has eaten the smallest bear’s porridge. She tries the chairs and beds while the bears are out. Read their three voices distinctly without shouting.

excerpt.locator: The Story of the Three Bears, 1922 edition pp. 20–22, paragraphs 4–14; begins “Then Goldilocks, who was tired, for she had been catching …” and ends “said the Little Wee Bear in his little wee voice.”.

questions.prompt: Does just right mean that the little chair can safely hold Goldilocks?
facilitatorNotes: No; the bottom breaks. A comfortable feeling does not guarantee that an object fits its use.
evidence: the bottom of the chair came out

questions.prompt: What makes the little bed different from the other beds for her?
facilitatorNotes: Neither end is too high, so she sleeps there. Ask the child to recall the repeated neither/nor form.
evidence: neither too high at the head, nor at the foot

questions.prompt: What does Little Wee Bear discover that the others do not?
facilitatorNotes: All his porridge is gone. The earlier action explains why his cry adds more words.
evidence: AND HAS EATEN IT ALL UP!

days.title: The Three Bears, part 3: following the evidence upstairs
days.workTitle: The Story of the Three Bears
days.challenge: Distinguish knowing that someone came from knowing who it was.
days.focus: A repeated cry grows into a direct discovery.
days.context: The bears have found their porridge eaten and their chairs disturbed. This part finishes the story. Truant means away from where one ought to be.
days.contentNote: The ending wonders whether Goldilocks broke her neck jumping from the window, got lost, or was whipped at home; the narrator says no one can say. Nothing is shown.

excerpt.locator: The Story of the Three Bears, 1922 edition pp. 22–24, paragraphs 15–35 (end); begins “Upon this the Three Bears, seeing that some one had …” and ends “… But the Three Bears never saw anything more of her.”.
excerpt.inlineReason: The night sets the display line “SOMEBODY HAS BEEN SITTING IN MY CHAIR, AND HAS SATE THE BOTTOM THROUGH!” as a two-line stanza broken before “THROUGH!”, following Project Gutenberg 17034’s line wrap; the 1922 print (p. 22) sets it as one line, so the library has it as a single paragraph and the night is not one contiguous range of the work.

blocks.text: Upon this the Three Bears, seeing that some one had entered their house, and eaten up the Little Wee Bear's breakfast, began to look about them. Now the careless Goldilocks had not put the hard cushion straight when she rose from the chair of the Great Big Bear.
"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN SITTING IN MY CHAIR!"
said the Great Big Bear in his great, rough, gruff voice.
And the careless Goldilocks had squatted down the soft cushion of the Middle-sized Bear.
"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN SITTING IN MY CHAIR!"
said the Middle-sized Bear in his middle-sized voice.

"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN SITTING IN MY CHAIR, AND HAS SATE THE BOTTOM
THROUGH!"
said the Little Wee Bear in his little wee voice.

Then the Three Bears thought they had better make further search in case it was a burglar, so they went upstairs into their bedchamber. Now Goldilocks had pulled the pillow of the Great Big Bear out of its place.
"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN LYING IN MY BED!"
said the Great Big Bear in his great, rough, gruff voice.
And Goldilocks had pulled the bolster of the Middle-sized Bear out of its place.
"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN LYING IN MY BED!"
said the Middle-sized Bear in his middle-sized voice.
But when the Little Wee Bear came to look at his bed, there was the bolster in its place!
And the pillow was in its place upon the bolster!
And upon the pillow----?
There was Goldilocks' yellow head--which was not in its place, for she had no business there.
"SOMEBODY HAS BEEN LYING IN MY BED,--AND HERE SHE IS STILL!"
said the Little Wee Bear in his little wee voice.

Now Goldilocks had heard in her sleep the great, rough, gruff voice of the Great Big Bear; but she was so fast asleep that it was no more to her than the roaring of wind, or the rumbling of thunder. And she had heard the middle-sized voice of the Middle-sized Bear, but it was only as if she had heard some one speaking in a dream. But when she heard the little wee voice of the Little Wee Bear, it was so sharp, and so shrill, that it awakened her at once. Up she started, and when she saw the Three Bears on one side of the bed, she tumbled herself out at the other, and ran to the window. Now the window was open, because the Bears, like good, tidy Bears, as they were, always opened their bedchamber window when they got up in the morning. So naughty, frightened little Goldilocks jumped; and whether she broke her neck in the fall, or ran into the wood and was lost there, or found her way out of the wood and got whipped for being a bad girl and playing truant no one can say. But the Three Bears never saw anything more of her.

questions.prompt: What clues do the large and middle bears find on their chairs?
facilitatorNotes: The cushions are moved or pressed down. Small changes reveal that somebody has sat there.
evidence: had not put the hard cushion straight

questions.prompt: The storyteller does not tell us what became of Goldilocks after she jumped. What possibilities does the storyteller list?
facilitatorNotes: She might have been hurt in the fall, lost in the wood, or found her way home and been punished; no one can say. The bears never see her again. Children may feel relief, worry, or satisfaction; accept a feeling tied to the words.
evidence: But the Three Bears never saw anything more of her.

questions.prompt: What changes in the last cry of Little Wee Bear?
facilitatorNotes: Here she is still replaces a guess about an absent somebody with a discovery of a present person. Read both cries to hear the change.
evidence: AND HERE SHE IS STILL!

days.title: Who has seen the wind?
days.challenge: Infer an unseen cause from two visible effects.
days.focus: Repeating a question leads to two signs of wind.
days.context: An adult reads each stanza, pausing for a gesture showing the leaves or trees.

excerpt.locator:
Who has seen the wind?; begins “Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:”; ends “But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.”.

questions.prompt: Can either person see the wind itself?
facilitatorNotes: Both answers say neither person can see it.
evidence: Neither I nor you:

questions.prompt: What do the leaves do when the wind passes?
facilitatorNotes: They tremble; fingers can show tiny shaking movements.
evidence: But when the leaves hang trembling

questions.prompt: How is the trees’ movement different from the leaves’ movement?
facilitatorNotes: The trees bow their heads, a larger bending action; both movements reveal the wind.
evidence: But when the trees bow down their heads

days.title: The Clever Hen
days.challenge: Separate realistic hen behaviour from the rhyme’s imaginative actions.
days.focus: An ordinary animal receives an extraordinary set of household abilities.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: The rhyme says the hen brews ale; ale is a kind of beer, part of this old household scene.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE CLEVER HEN”; opening “I had a little hen, the prettiest ever seen,”; ending “She sat by the fire and told many a fine tale.”.

questions.prompt: What does the hen fetch from the mill?
facilitatorNotes: Flour, which she brings home quickly. Explain a mill as a place that grinds grain.
evidence: She went to the mill to fetch me some flour,

questions.prompt: Choose one job in the poem that makes this hen wonderfully unlike a real hen.
facilitatorNotes: Washing dishes, baking bread or telling tales all work; ask for the matching words rather than one mandatory choice.
evidence: She washed me the dishes and kept the house clean;

questions.prompt: After all the jobs, how does the hen spend time beside the fire?
facilitatorNotes: She tells many fine tales. The ending changes from work to a companionable story time.
evidence: She sat by the fire and told many a fine tale.

days.title: The Star
days.challenge: Listen beyond the familiar opening to the star’s imagined work.
days.focus: The speaker links a bright image to help for a traveler.
days.context: Read all five stanzas; “trav’ller” means traveler. The poem predates modern explanations available to children today.

excerpt.locator:
The Star; begins “Twinkle, twinkle, little star,”; ends “Though I know not what you are,
Twinkle, twinkle, little star.”.

questions.prompt: What sparkling thing does the first stanza compare the star to?
facilitatorNotes: A diamond helps us picture a bright point of light.
evidence: Like a diamond in the sky.

questions.prompt: Who is helped by the star in the dark?
facilitatorNotes: The traveler is grateful for its tiny spark.
evidence: Then the trav’ller in the dark

questions.prompt: Why might the child call the star’s light a tiny eye?
facilitatorNotes: It appears to watch or peek through the curtains. Treat the image as imagination.
evidence: And often through my curtains peep,

days.title: The Woodpecker’s Nest, part 1: a laughing cry
days.challenge: Use sound first, then sight, to identify an animal.
days.focus: Patient watching lets the children describe the bird’s colours, tongue, tail and toes.
days.context: Peter, Peggy and Paul are country children who watch wild animals on the way to school. They see a green woodpecker, a British bird; yaffil is a country name for its call. A thrush is a common songbird, used here for size.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Woodpecker’s Nest, printed pages 10–11, paragraphs 1–7; begins “We were lying under the shade of the trees in …” and ends “… himself. Then he spread his wings and flew slowly away.”.

questions.prompt: How do the children know a woodpecker is near before they see it?
facilitatorNotes: They hear its strange laughing cry, and Peggy names the bird. Invite the child to say the call aloud.
evidence: It was like someone laughing, "Yaffil, Yaffil, Yaffil."

questions.prompt: How does the woodpecker use its stiff tail?
facilitatorNotes: He bends it against the tree to push himself up, and later comes down tail first to steady himself. Either use is correct.
evidence: he bent it against the tree, and pushed himself up

questions.prompt: Peggy says the bird is eating ants. What did the children see that led to that idea?
facilitatorNotes: A long shining tongue that darted out and back. Peggy adds that the tip is sticky; distinguish what they saw from her explanation.
evidence: a long shining tongue came out of his mouth

days.title: The Woodpecker’s Nest, part 2: inside the old elm
days.challenge: Put the events of several weeks in order.
days.focus: Repeated visits let the children follow eggs, chicks, and an empty nest.
days.context: The children watched a woodpecker climb a tree and fly away; now they follow it. “Give me a back” means bend over so a friend can climb on. Children of that time often handled wild nests; today wild birds’ nests and eggs are protected by law.
days.contentNote: Peter takes the mother bird and her eggs out of the nest, lets her go, and puts the eggs back; the young birds hatch and fly away.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Woodpecker’s Nest, printed pages 11–14, paragraphs 8–17 (end of lesson); begins “We crept after him, and by-and-by he stopped at an …” and ends “… gone. Peter climbed up and found the nest quite empty.”.

questions.prompt: How does Peter reach the woodpecker’s hole?
facilitatorNotes: He climbs on Paul’s back to reach the branches, then holds the boughs and creeps round the trunk.
evidence: So Paul let Peter climb on his back

questions.prompt: What does Paul say will happen if the eggs go back into the nest?
facilitatorNotes: The mother will return and sit on them, and they can come back to see the young birds. Children may also discuss whether taking them out was a good idea.
evidence: then the mother will fly back and sit on them

questions.prompt: How do the children learn that the young birds have grown up and left?
facilitatorNotes: The parents carry insects in, the young birds come out on the tree, a week later they are flying, and then the nest is empty. Ask for the steps in order.
evidence: found the nest quite empty.

days.title: Two Birds
days.challenge: Track a changing scene while joining the unchanged refrain.
days.focus: A repeated refrain frames two departures and a suddenly empty place.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “TWO BIRDS”; opening “There were two birds sat on a stone,”; ending “Fa, la, la, la, lal, de.”.

questions.prompt: Where do the birds sit at the beginning?
facilitatorNotes: On a stone. Use two fingers resting on a hand as a simple model if the child wishes.
evidence: There were two birds sat on a stone,

questions.prompt: What changes after the other bird follows the first?
facilitatorNotes: No birds remain. The stone is left alone, which makes the empty ending noticeable.
evidence:
The other bird flew after,
And then there was none,

questions.prompt: Which playful sounds keep returning even as the birds leave?
facilitatorNotes: Fa, la, la, la, lal, de is repeated. Invite the child to join it; it supplies music rather than new plot information.
evidence: Fa, la, la, la, lal, de;

days.title: March
days.challenge: Follow a conversation between Spring and hidden flowers.
days.focus: Seasonal change becomes a scene of waiting and reassurance.
days.context: Spring and Winter act like people in this poem. The flowers begin beneath the ground.

excerpt.locator:
March; begins “IN the snowing and the blowing,”; ends “Soon my birds shall sing above you,--
Set you free at last."”.

questions.prompt: Where are the flowers growing at the beginning?
facilitatorNotes: They are beneath the listeners’ feet, not yet above the ground.
evidence: Far beneath our feet.

questions.prompt: Who taps and asks whether the flowers are there?
facilitatorNotes: Spring speaks gently to them.
evidence: Softly taps the Spring, and cheerly,--

questions.prompt: What promise tells the flowers that winter will end?
facilitatorNotes: Spring says Winter is going and birds will sing overhead; accept either connected sign.
evidence:
He is going,
Going on his way.

days.title: Lucy Locket
days.challenge: Distinguish finding the pocket from finding anything inside it.
days.focus: A lost object is found, but its contents are unexpectedly absent.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “LUCY LOCKET”; opening “Lucy Locket lost her pocket,”; ending “But the binding round it.”.

questions.prompt: Who loses the pocket, and who finds it?
facilitatorNotes: Lucy Locket loses it; Kitty Fisher finds it. A pocket here can be an older detachable pouch.
evidence:
Lucy Locket lost her pocket,
Kitty Fisher found it;

questions.prompt: Is there money or a toy inside the found pocket?
facilitatorNotes: The poem says nothing is in it. Do not supply imagined contents as fact.
evidence: Nothing in it, nothing in it,

questions.prompt: What does the last line leave us noticing around the empty pocket?
facilitatorNotes: Its binding, the edging around it. The repeated nothing makes that nearly empty answer comic.
evidence: But the binding round it.

days.title: Bed in Summer
days.challenge: Compare the child’s bedtime in winter and summer.
days.focus: Bright outdoor life explains a child’s complaint.
days.context: The speaker lives where summer evenings stay light longer than winter evenings.

excerpt.locator:
Bed in Summer; begins “IN winter I get up at night
And dress by yellow candle-light.”; ends “And I should like so much to play,
To have to go to bed by day?”.

questions.prompt: What lights the child’s winter morning?
facilitatorNotes: Yellow candlelight suggests it is still dark outdoors.
evidence: And dress by yellow candle-light.

questions.prompt: Name one thing still happening outside at summer bedtime.
facilitatorNotes: Birds are hopping and grown-ups’ feet are passing in the street.
evidence: Or hear the grown-up people's feet

questions.prompt: Why does the child think this bedtime is hard?
facilitatorNotes: The sky is still clear and blue and the child wants to play. No judgment about the family rule is required.
evidence: And I should like so much to play,

days.title: Of Sending Cheeses: food that cannot follow directions
days.challenge: Distinguish movement caused by a hill from purposeful travel.
days.focus: The storyteller lets listeners see a mistaken explanation before the character does.
days.context: Gotham is a village in a group of old comic tales. A wallet here is a carrying bag. The man intends to sell cheese at a market down the hill.

excerpt.locator: The Wise Men of Gotham: Of Sending Cheeses, 1922 edition pp. 292–293, complete; begins “There was a man of Gotham who went to the …” and ends “… this day no man can tell him of his cheeses.”.

questions.prompt: What accident gives the man his strange idea?
facilitatorNotes: One cheese falls and rolls downhill. He mistakes gravity-driven movement for choosing to travel.
evidence: rolled down the hill.

questions.prompt: Where do the cheeses actually go after he releases them?
facilitatorNotes: Into bushes. The listener knows this even while the man expects to meet them at market.
evidence: Some went into one bush, and some went into another.

questions.prompt: How does his explanation become even more unlikely at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He decides the cheeses have gone all the way to York and rents a horse to follow. He keeps the mistaken idea rather than checking the bushes.
evidence: hired a horse to ride to York

days.title: Pussy-Cat and Queen
days.challenge: Compare the announced purpose of a visit with the action reported afterward.
days.focus: Question-and-answer exchanges reveal a cat’s very catlike interest.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PUSSY-CAT AND QUEEN”; opening “"Pussy-cat, pussy-cat,”; ending “Under the chair."”.

questions.prompt: Where has Pussy-cat been, and whom did it go to see?
facilitatorNotes: London, to look at the Queen. Use two voices to distinguish questions from answers.
evidence:
I've been to London
    To look at the Queen.

questions.prompt: What small creature becomes important in the second answer?
facilitatorNotes: A little mouse under a chair. The poem moves from the grand Queen to a small mouse.
evidence:
I frightened a little mouse
    Under the chair.

questions.prompt: Does Pussy-cat tell us what the Queen said or did?
facilitatorNotes: No; the cat tells about frightening the mouse instead. Accept amusement that a royal visit becomes an ordinary cat-and-mouse moment.
evidence: What did you there?

days.title: A white hen sitting
days.challenge: Track a change from eggs to chicks and then a protective action.
days.focus: Repeated phrases emphasize plumpness and safety.
days.context: Read and invite the child to show three eggs with fingers.

excerpt.locator:
A white hen sitting; begins “A white hen sitting
On white eggs three:”; ends “But chicks beneath their mother’s wing
Squat safe as safe can be.”.

questions.prompt: What appears after the three eggs?
facilitatorNotes: Three speckled chickens appear; the number stays three.
evidence: Next, three speckled chickens

questions.prompt: Where do the chicks go when visitors arrive?
facilitatorNotes: They crouch beneath their mother’s wing.
evidence: But chicks beneath their mother’s wing

questions.prompt: Which repeated words make the ending feel reassuring?
facilitatorNotes: “Safe as safe can be” emphasizes protection. Invite the child to hear the repetition.
evidence: Squat safe as safe can be.

days.title: The Winds
days.challenge: Recognise an impossible detail rather than treating every statement as a fact.
days.focus: Compass directions become dinner guests in a nonsense miniature.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE WINDS”; opening “Mister East gave a feast;”; ending “Eating cold potato.”.

questions.prompt: Who gives the feast, and who lays the cloth?
facilitatorNotes: Mister East gives the feast; Mister North lays the cloth. Let the child assign the two roles to gestures.
evidence:
Mister East gave a feast;
Mister North laid the cloth;

questions.prompt: What happens to Mister South’s mouth?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme says he burns it while eating a cold potato. Reread the last two lines together.
evidence:
Mister South burnt his mouth
Eating cold potato.

questions.prompt: Why is the cold potato a surprising ending?
facilitatorNotes: Cold food would not normally burn from heat. The contradiction is a nonsense joke, not food or science advice.
evidence: Eating cold potato.

days.title: Boats sail on the rivers
days.challenge: Compare objects on water with images in the sky.
days.focus: The poem turns clouds into travelers and a rainbow into a bridge.
days.context: Here “bow” means rainbow and “heaven” means sky. Read once, then gesture across an imagined sky.

excerpt.locator:
Boats sail on the rivers; begins “Boats sail on the rivers,
And ships sail on the seas;”; ends “And builds a road from earth to sky,
Is prettier far than these.”.

questions.prompt: What sails in the sky in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: Clouds are described as sailing, like the boats below.
evidence: But clouds that sail across the sky

questions.prompt: Which bridge reaches above the trees?
facilitatorNotes: The rainbow, not a built river bridge, overtops them.
evidence: And overtops the trees,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker prefer the river sights or the sky sights?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker calls clouds and the rainbow prettier; a child may have a different preference but should distinguish it from the speaker’s.
evidence: Is prettier far than these.

days.title: Just Like Me
days.challenge: Hear how the same response can fit actions and then unexpectedly suggest likeness.
days.focus: A repeated answer becomes a joke when its meaning shifts.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “JUST LIKE ME”; opening “"I went up one pair of stairs."”; ending “"Just like me."”.

questions.prompt: What two climbs does the first voice describe?
facilitatorNotes: Going up one pair of stairs, then two pairs. The second voice keeps agreeing that it did the same.
evidence: I went up two pairs of stairs.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker look out of before seeing the monkey?
facilitatorNotes: A window. Retell the room and window actions in their given order.
evidence: I looked out of a window.

questions.prompt: Why might the last “Just like me” make listeners laugh?
facilitatorNotes: After the monkey is named, the reply can sound as if the responder resembles a monkey. Accept noticing this playful double meaning rather than insisting on it.
evidence: And there I saw a monkey.

days.title: The little Girl to her Dolly
days.challenge: Follow pretend nighttime changing into pretend morning.
days.focus: A child borrows a caregiver’s words and routines during play.
days.context: The child is pretending to be a doll’s mother. “Crumb you a mess” means prepare a little food from crumbs.

excerpt.locator: The little Girl to her Dolly; begins “There, go to sleep, Dolly, in own mother’s lap;”; ends “For I think it high time to have done with bye bye.”.

questions.prompt: What does the girl pretend her lap has become?
facilitatorNotes: She explicitly makes believe that it is Dolly’s bed.
evidence: And then make believe that my lap is your bed;

questions.prompt: What words does she repeat while settling Dolly?
facilitatorNotes: “Bye bye” repeats as a soothing bedtime phrase. The listener can join the second occurrence.
evidence: Bye bye, little Dolly, lie still, and bye bye.

questions.prompt: What new action shows that the pretend night is over?
facilitatorNotes: She wakes the doll and offers food in its china cup.
evidence: There, now it is morning, and time to get up,

days.title: Tom Kitten, part 1: clothes for company
days.challenge: Distinguish what kittens naturally do from the mother’s formal expectations.
days.focus: Clothing creates the story’s physical problem.
days.context: Three kittens are being prepared for their mother’s visitors. Pinafores and tuckers are pieces of clothing. The tale is read in three parts on three nights.
days.contentNote: The historical narrator calls Tom fat and naughty. Discuss clothing fit and actions without using body size as a judgment about children.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Tom Kitten, paragraphs 1–10; begins “Once upon a time there were three little kittens, and …” and ends “… out of the way while she made hot buttered toast.”.

questions.prompt: What do the kittens do before their mother brings them indoors?
facilitatorNotes: They tumble at the doorstep and play in dust. Connect their ordinary play to the mother’s wish for clean formal clothing.
evidence: they tumbled about the doorstep and played in the dust.

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Tabitha wash and dress them?
facilitatorNotes: She expects friends for tea. The preparation belongs to a social visit, not a change the kittens requested.
evidence: expected friends to tea

questions.prompt: Which word tells us the elegant clothes do not feel good to Tom?
facilitatorNotes: Uncomfortable. Ask how something can look fine while feeling awkward.
evidence: elegant uncomfortable clothes

days.title: Tom Kitten, part 2: climbing in trousers
days.challenge: Retell how movement makes the carefully arranged clothes fall apart.
days.focus: The comedy depends on a mismatch between kitten bodies and formal dress.
days.context: The kittens have been dressed for visitors and sent into the garden. This continues the previous excerpt. A rockery is a garden area with rocks and plants.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Tom Kitten, paragraphs 11–18; begins “"Now keep your frocks clean, children! You must walk on …” and ends “… hat fell off, and the rest of his buttons burst.”.

questions.prompt: What does their mother want them to keep clean?
facilitatorNotes: Their frocks, or dresses. They are also told to avoid several dirty places.
evidence: Now keep your frocks clean, children!

questions.prompt: What happens when Moppet and Mittens tread on their pinafores?
facilitatorNotes: They fall on their noses and get green smears. Connect the long clothing with the stumble.
evidence: they trod upon their pinafores and fell on their noses.

questions.prompt: Why is reaching the wall especially difficult for Tom?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot jump normally while upright in trousers, and his clothes lose buttons. Invite a safe gesture showing the imagined difficulty rather than acting out a fall.
evidence: Tom Kitten was quite unable to jump when walking upon his hind legs in trousers.

days.title: Tom Kitten, part 3: the ducks dress themselves
days.challenge: Follow two surprises at the end: where the clothes go, and what the mother tells her visitors.
days.focus: Comic reversals finish the tale: the ducks take the clothes, and the mother’s tidy plan collapses.
days.context: The kittens are on the garden wall with their clothes coming loose. The Puddle-ducks are walking along the road. This part finishes the tale. Affronted means embarrassed and offended; the measles is an illness that keeps children in bed.
days.contentNote: Mrs. Tabitha smacks the kittens and tells her guests an untrue excuse; the narrator says plainly that it was not true. This was ordinary nursery discipline in 1907 and can be discussed as part of the story.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Tom Kitten, paragraphs 19–37 (end); begins “While they were in difficulties, there was a pit pat …” and ends “… Jemima and Rebeccah, have been looking for them ever since.”.

questions.prompt: Which words let us hear the ducks coming along the road?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated pit pat, paddle pat imitate feet on the hard road. Invite the child to repeat the rhythm and notice that it returns when the ducks leave.
evidence: pit pat paddle pat!

questions.prompt: Moppet asks Mr. Drake to button up Tom. What does he do with the clothes instead?
facilitatorNotes: He puts them on himself and walks off with the other ducks. Contrast what Moppet asked for with what happens; the narrator adds that they fit him even worse than Tom.
evidence: But he put them on _himself!_

questions.prompt: Mrs. Tabitha tells her friends the kittens are in bed with the measles. How does the storyteller let us know that is not true?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says so directly and adds that they were not in bed at all; noises overhead disturb the tea party. Children may suggest why she said it, such as embarrassment; accept reasons tied to the text.
evidence: which was not true.
they were not in bed: _not_ in the least.

days.title: Mary’s Canary
days.challenge: Combine visual and sound details into a picture of the bird.
days.focus: Colour and song establish a listener’s affection for a small bird.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: The poem describes a pet bird kept in a cage; discussion may acknowledge that real birds have care needs.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “MARY'S CANARY”; opening “Mary had a pretty bird,”; ending “Sat hearing her canary.”.

questions.prompt: What colour are the canary’s feathers?
facilitatorNotes: Bright yellow. Invite the child to describe or point to that colour without needing an illustration.
evidence: Feathers bright and yellow,

questions.prompt: Which feature delights Mary: the cage or the bird’s song?
facilitatorNotes: The sweet note delights her. The cage is where the bird is kept, not the thing she is said to enjoy hearing.
evidence: The sweetest note he always sung,

questions.prompt: What does Mary do that shows she enjoys the canary’s company?
facilitatorNotes: She often sits nearby hearing it. Repeated visits support an inference of pleasure or affection.
evidence: Sat hearing her canary.

days.title: Burs
days.challenge: Hold a series of imagined constructions in mind.
days.focus: Sticky seeds become a shared building material in playful verse.
days.context: Burs are prickly seed coverings that cling. Picture the making together; no gathering or handling is needed.

excerpt.locator:
Burs; begins “DEAR me!
What shall it be?”; ends “Ah, how we love 'em,
These comical burs!”.

questions.prompt: What feature of burs makes all this building possible?
facilitatorNotes: They stick closely together.
evidence:
See how they fasten
Close to each other!

questions.prompt: How do the builders divide the work on their cottage?
facilitatorNotes: One does the roof and the other the floors; the speaker gives these jobs.
evidence:
You do the roof,
And I'll do the floors.

questions.prompt: Which proposed creation surprised you most, and which words made you picture it?
facilitatorNotes: Accept any named creation with a detail from the poem, including pancake, hat, or cottage.
evidence: Let's make a pancake,--

days.title: The Little Bird
days.challenge: Contrast what the speaker wants with what the bird actually does.
days.focus: A child’s invitation meets a wild bird’s independent movement.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE LITTLE BIRD”; opening “Once I saw a little bird”; ending “And far away he flew.”.

questions.prompt: How does the bird move before it flies?
facilitatorNotes: It hops. The repeated hop lets listeners act or hear the small movements.
evidence: Come hop, hop, hop;

questions.prompt: What does the child want the bird to do?
facilitatorNotes: Stop so the child can greet it. Repeat stop in the same rhythm as hop to hear the parallel.
evidence: Will you stop, stop, stop?

questions.prompt: Does the bird stay for the greeting? Tell how the poem ends.
facilitatorNotes: It shakes its tail and flies far away. The child’s wish does not control the bird.
evidence: And far away he flew.

days.title: Singing
days.challenge: Hear a shared action connecting different places and singers.
days.focus: The repeated idea of singing widens from a bird to distant children and an instrument.
days.context: An organ man played a portable street instrument. Japan and Spain are countries named in the poem.

excerpt.locator:
Singing; begins “OF speckled eggs the birdie sings
And nests among the trees;”; ends “The organ with the organ man
Is singing in the rain.”.

questions.prompt: What does the bird sing about?
facilitatorNotes: Speckled eggs and nests are its subjects.
evidence: OF speckled eggs the birdie sings

questions.prompt: Which two countries are named as places where children sing?
facilitatorNotes: Japan and Spain connect the local picture with other places; the adult supplies the names.
evidence:
The children sing in far Japan,
The children sing in Spain;

questions.prompt: Why is it interesting to say the organ is “singing”?
facilitatorNotes: An instrument makes music without a human singing voice; the same word links all the sounds.
evidence: Is singing in the rain.

days.title: Spring Flowers, part 1: daffodils and wind-flowers
days.challenge: Compare two flowers part by part.
days.focus: Description by contrast: leaves, flower shape, and how each plant responds to weather.
days.context: In England, wild daffodils and wood-anemones bloom in early spring. “Lent lilies” is a local name for daffodils. A bulb is an underground food store, like an onion.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Spring Flowers, printed pages 14–15, paragraphs 1–4; begins “We are always glad when April comes. Then we can …” and ends “… shuts up in a tight bud, till sunshine comes again.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the children glad when April comes?
facilitatorNotes: Many more flowers appear on their way to school; before April there are only a few. Accept either part of the contrast.
evidence: We are always glad when April comes.

questions.prompt: What does the wood-anemone do when the clouds gather and rain falls?
facilitatorNotes: It shuts into a tight bud until the sun comes back. Contrast it with the open pink and white cup in sunshine.
evidence: it shuts up in a tight bud, till sunshine comes again.

questions.prompt: Paul says the daffodil blooms early because of its bulb. How does he explain it?
facilitatorNotes: It stores food in the bulb in autumn and uses it in January to make leaves and flowers. This is Paul’s explanation; let the child retell it.
evidence: It stores up food in the bulb in the autumn.

days.title: Spring Flowers, part 2: where the honey hides
days.challenge: Follow a description that explains how a plant works.
days.focus: Close looking explains how leaves carry water and where bees find honey.
days.context: Primroses and violets are small wild spring flowers. The flower’s “honey” is nectar, which bees gather. Children at that time tasted leaves and flowers; many wild plants, including the anemone in this lesson, are poisonous.
days.contentNote: Peggy bites a poisonous leaf, and the children suck flower parts to taste the nectar.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Spring Flowers, printed pages 15–17, paragraphs 5–10 (end of lesson); begins “Peggy once bit one of the leaves of the anemone. …” and ends “… can now find plenty of honey to fill their hives.”.

questions.prompt: What happened when Peggy bit an anemone leaf, and what did Paul tell her?
facilitatorNotes: It burned her tongue and tasted bitter; Paul said the plant is poisonous, which is why animals leave it alone.
evidence: It burnt her tongue and tasted very bitter.

questions.prompt: How do the bumpy primrose leaves help the plant drink?
facilitatorNotes: Their hills and valleys guide rainwater down to the roots. A hand cupped into a channel can show the idea.
evidence: These guide it down to the roots

questions.prompt: Where is the violet’s honey, and how does a bee reach it?
facilitatorNotes: In a small bag or spur behind the flower; the bee pushes her head into the yellow beak and sips with her tongue.
evidence: she sips out the honey with her tongue from the bag or spur behind the flower.

days.title: A Cherry
days.challenge: Use the title and two physical clues to solve a playful riddle.
days.focus: A familiar fruit is hidden under a person-like description.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “A CHERRY”; opening “As I went through the garden gap,”; ending “If you'll tell me this riddle, I'll give you a groat.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker meet the mysterious Dick Red-cap?
facilitatorNotes: At or through the garden gap. The garden setting helps prepare a fruit answer.
evidence: As I went through the garden gap,

questions.prompt: If the answer is a cherry, what might its stick and stone really be?
facilitatorNotes: The stick can be its stalk and the stone its pit. Present this as solving the figurative clues, not a person swallowing a stone.
evidence: A stick in his hand, a stone in his throat,

questions.prompt: What reward does the speaker promise for solving the riddle?
facilitatorNotes: A groat, an old coin. The promise makes the rhyme sound like a little guessing game between speaker and listener.
evidence: I'll give you a groat.

days.title: The Field Daisy
days.challenge: Identify a flower through its imagined self-description.
days.focus: A daisy speaks about its shape and asks for gentle footsteps.
days.context: The title tells us the speaker is a daisy. “O’er” means over.

excerpt.locator: The Field Daisy; begins “I’m a pretty little thing,”; ends ““Surly Winter’s gone away.””.

questions.prompt: What is the daisy’s white-and-yellow “hat”?
facilitatorNotes: Its flower head has white petals and a yellow center; a drawing can express this.
evidence: With a white and yellow hat.

questions.prompt: What does the daisy ask the passing child not to do?
facilitatorNotes: It asks not to be stepped on.
evidence: Skip about, but do not tread

questions.prompt: Why might seeing this daisy suggest that winter is over?
facilitatorNotes: It says it comes with spring; the closing words echo that beginning.
evidence: Always coming with the spring;

days.title: Chorus of Fairies
days.challenge: Follow several settings while hearing recurring words and sound patterns.
days.focus: Repeated summer-day lines give a landscape poem a singing chorus.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “CHORUS OF FAIRIES.”; opening “GOLDEN, golden,”; ending “All the livelong Summer day!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 23.

questions.prompt: Where do the fairies work and play? Name two places.
facilitatorNotes: Flowery meadows and forest shadows are stated; hill, valley and sea-spray appear later. Accept any two actual locations.
evidence:
In flowery meadows,
          And forest shadows,

questions.prompt: Which words make their movement sound light and lively?
facilitatorNotes: Sprightly and lightly, or busily and merrily, work. Echo a chosen pair and ask what sort of movement it suggests.
evidence: Sprightly, lightly,

questions.prompt: What stretch of time keeps returning at the ends of the verses?
facilitatorNotes: The length of a summer day. The repeated phrase holds the changing scenes together like a song refrain.
evidence: All the length of a Summer day!

days.title: Lawkamercyme: a puzzling recognition test
days.challenge: Follow how one mistaken test leads to an impossible conclusion.
days.focus: A refrain turns confusion about appearance into a comic identity puzzle.
days.context: This old rhyme uses Lawkamercyme as an exclamation, rather like goodness me. A pedlar sells goods while traveling; petticoats are skirts worn beneath other clothing.
days.contentNote: A stranger damages the sleeping woman’s clothing. Treat that as unkind conduct, while exploring the rhyme’s comic confusion.

excerpt.locator: Lawkamercyme, 1922 edition pp. 331–332, complete; begins “There was an old woman, as I've heard tell, / …” and ends “… began to cry-- / "Lawkamercyme! this is none of I!"”.

questions.prompt: What does the woman plan to sell, and what interrupts her trip?
facilitatorNotes: She takes eggs to market but falls asleep on the road. Establish the setting before discussing the strange change.
evidence: her eggs for to sell

questions.prompt: What has changed when she wakes?
facilitatorNotes: Someone has cut her skirts shorter, and she is cold. Her clothes have changed; she remains the same person.
evidence: He cut her petticoats up to the knees

questions.prompt: Why is a barking dog a poor way to decide who she is?
facilitatorNotes: Dogs can bark for many reasons, especially at night. The rhyme gives her conclusion, but listeners can question the test that led to it.
evidence: If it be I, he'll wag his little tail

days.title: Little Green Hummer
days.challenge: Picture rapid movement using a chain of short phrases.
days.focus: Jewel colors and quick rhythms describe a hummingbird.
days.context: This is the hummingbird poem in “Garden Songs.” Some phrases are imaginative exaggeration: a real bird weighs more than one feather.

excerpt.locator:
Little Green Hummer; begins “LITTLE green Hummer
Was born in the summer;”; ends “This sweet little Hummer
That came with the summer.”.

questions.prompt: What color is Hummer’s coat, and what shining thing does it resemble?
facilitatorNotes: Green and emerald are paired; jewel is another later comparison.
evidence: As the emerald's light.

questions.prompt: What words show Hummer moving around a blossom?
facilitatorNotes: Over, under, and in make a changing route the child can trace.
evidence:
Now over a blossom,
Now under, now in it;

questions.prompt: Does the poem make Hummer seem slow or quick?
facilitatorNotes: “All in a minute” and “darted” support quick; reread the short phrases at a lively but clear pace.
evidence:
Here, there, and everywhere,
All in a minute.

days.title: Amy Margaret
days.challenge: Move from literal age and hair to comparisons that describe character.
days.focus: Flower and jewel images express affection for a named child.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “AMY MARGARET.”; opening “AMY MARGARET'S five years old,”; ending “Be ever,--Amy Margaret!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 26.

questions.prompt: How old is Amy Margaret, and what colour is her hair called?
facilitatorNotes: She is five and her hair is gold. Gold can describe a yellow hair colour here.
evidence:
AMY MARGARET'S five years old,
    Amy Margaret's hair is gold,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker say gold is more precious than Amy?
facilitatorNotes: No; Amy is described as far dearer than gold. The very large number expresses affection rather than a price.
evidence:
Dearer twenty-thousand-fold
          Than gold, is Amy Margaret.

questions.prompt: What three things is Amy compared with near the end?
facilitatorNotes: A friend, a daisy and a pearl. Let the child choose which comparison sounds kind, fresh or precious and explain; several readings fit.
evidence: A friend, a daisy, and a pearl;

days.title: My Bed Is a Boat
days.challenge: Connect details of an ordinary bed with an imagined voyage.
days.focus: An extended comparison turns falling asleep into travel.
days.context: A nurse here is a caregiver. “Embark” means begin a boat journey; “fast” at the end means secured.

questions.prompt: What familiar object is the child imagining as a boat?
facilitatorNotes: The bed becomes the boat while the room supplies its setting.
evidence: MY bed is a little boat;

questions.prompt: What does the child take aboard for the night?
facilitatorNotes: Toys and perhaps a slice of wedding cake travel with the child.
evidence: Perhaps a toy or two.

questions.prompt: What tells you that the child is safe at the end of this voyage?
facilitatorNotes: Morning brings the child back to the room and the vessel is secured.
evidence: Safe in my room, beside the pier,

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 1: rain and a fishing plan
days.challenge: Infer why weather pleasant to a frog might seem unpleasant to a person.
days.focus: Human clothing and tools are imaginatively fitted to pond life.
days.context: Jeremy is a storybook frog preparing a meal for friends. A macintosh is a raincoat; goloshes are waterproof overshoes; minnows are small fish.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 1–10; begins “Once upon a time there was a frog called Mr. …” and ends “… and he tied a little wriggling worm at the end.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jeremy enjoy his wet home?
facilitatorNotes: He likes wet feet and is comfortable in dampness. This is a fictional frog’s viewpoint, not advice about staying in wet clothes.
evidence: Mr. Jeremy liked getting his feet wet

questions.prompt: What must happen before he will invite his friends?
facilitatorNotes: He plans to invite them if he catches more than five fish. Let the child explain his plan without turning discussion into a counting test.
evidence: If I catch more than five fish, I will invite my friends

questions.prompt: What familiar pond object does his boat resemble?
facilitatorNotes: A lily leaf. Notice how a small frog can use pond materials as people use boats and rods.
evidence: very like the other lily-leaves.

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 2: a troublesome catch
days.challenge: Follow the difference between what Jeremy hopes for and what he catches.
days.focus: Small surprises build from a tickled toe to a prickly fish.
days.context: Jeremy has anchored his leaf-like boat and waited for fish. A stickleback is a small fish with sharp spines; rushes are tall waterside plants.
days.contentNote: A fish’s spines prick Jeremy’s fingers; no graphic injury is described.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 11–23; begins “The rain trickled down his back, and for nearly an …” and ends “… put their heads out, and laughed at Mr. Jeremy Fisher.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Jeremy stop waiting and take a break?
facilitatorNotes: He has waited nearly an hour and wants lunch. Invite the child to use the time and his spoken complaint.
evidence: This is getting tiresome, I think I should like some lunch

questions.prompt: How does Jeremy protect his toes without stopping lunch?
facilitatorNotes: He draws his legs up out of reach. Trace the beetle’s action and Jeremy’s response.
evidence: Mr. Jeremy crossed his legs up shorter, out of reach

questions.prompt: Why is the fish he catches a surprise?
facilitatorNotes: He expects a smooth minnow but catches a spiny stickleback that pricks and escapes. Accept a contrast of the two descriptions.
evidence: Instead of a smooth fat minnow, Mr. Jeremy landed little Jack Sharp the stickleback, covered with spines!

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 3: a different dinner
days.challenge: Connect the raincoat introduced earlier to the escape.
days.focus: A frightening reversal ends in a comic change of menu.
days.context: Jeremy has had no success fishing and is sitting in his boat. Listen for how the raincoat helps him. The animal friends’ meal is fantasy, not a recipe.
days.contentNote: Brief fantasy peril: a trout catches Jeremy, then immediately spits him out. Jeremy reaches home safely.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 24–33 (end); begins “And while Mr. Jeremy sat disconsolately on the edge of …” and ends “… beautiful treat; but _I_ think it must have been nasty!”.

questions.prompt: Why does the trout spit Jeremy out?
facilitatorNotes: It dislikes the taste of his raincoat. The coat becomes unexpectedly useful in a new way.
evidence: the trout was so displeased with the taste of the macintosh

questions.prompt: What does Jeremy decide about fishing after he escapes?
facilitatorNotes: He does not expect to dare go fishing again. Accept fear or relief supported by his words.
evidence: I am sure I should never have dared to go fishing again!

questions.prompt: How can the friends still have dinner without the minnows?
facilitatorNotes: Jeremy has other food and the tortoise brings salad. Notice how the narrator dislikes the menu even though the frogs enjoy it.
evidence: Mr. Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise brought a salad with him in a string bag.

days.title: Dreaming
days.challenge: Track the imagined journey into sleep and the sudden return on waking.
days.focus: A dream becomes a travelling visitor that opens an impossible world.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “DREAMING.”; opening “A STRANGE little Dream”; ending “For its end could never be found.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 30, 31.

questions.prompt: How does the little Dream reach sleeping Fred?
facilitatorNotes: It comes down a long star-beam and slips under his eyelids. Treat this as a fantasy picture, not an explanation of sleep.
evidence: On a long star-beam

questions.prompt: Choose one sight that tells you this new world can do impossible things.
facilitatorNotes: Floating without wings, a speaking beast or a rope from the moon all work. Ask the child to name the particular sight.
evidence: And Floating in Air without wings,

questions.prompt: Why is the end of the moon-rope never found?
facilitatorNotes: Fred wakes too soon. The waking cuts off the dream’s unfinished discovery.
evidence:
Fred woke too soon,
    For its end could never be found.

days.title: A house of cards
days.challenge: Notice how the same action changes from a warning into an invitation.
days.focus: Building and falling are both parts of the speaker’s play.
days.context: Court cards are the picture cards in a pack. Read both references to shaking the table.

excerpt.locator:
A house of cards; begins “A house of cards
Is neat and small:”; ends “Shake the table!
That’s the fun.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to this house if the table shakes?
facilitatorNotes: The card house falls because its balance is disturbed.
evidence: It must fall.

questions.prompt: Which words tell the builder to add the top of the house?
facilitatorNotes: “Roof it” names adding the roof.
evidence: Raise it, roof it,—

questions.prompt: Does the ending sound upset about the falling house?
facilitatorNotes: No: the speaker calls it fun and gives the shaking command enthusiastically.
evidence: That’s the fun.

days.title: I Love You, Dear
days.challenge: Compare the butterfly wish, bird wish and final real gift.
days.focus: Imagined animal forms turn affection into actions of staying close.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “I LOVE YOU, DEAR.”; opening “I LOVE you, Dear, I love you, Dear,”; ending “And my love along with this, you Dear!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 32.

questions.prompt: If the speaker became a butterfly, what would it do near the loved person?
facilitatorNotes: Waver around and above them. Invite a hand movement that follows those position words.
evidence: I'd waver around and above you, Dear.

questions.prompt: How would being a bird offer a different way to show affection?
facilitatorNotes: The bird would sing beside the person every day. Compare flying nearby with providing song.
evidence: I'd sing every day beside you, Dear,

questions.prompt: At the end, what gift carries the speaker’s love without needing to become an animal?
facilitatorNotes: A flower is offered with love. The kiss is also mentioned, but the question’s gift is the flower.
evidence: This flow'r for my sake,

days.title: Rain
days.challenge: Hold a near place and a far place in one small picture.
days.focus: Four lines expand the rain’s reach beyond the speaker.
days.context: Read slowly twice; the listener may point nearby for umbrellas and far away for ships.

excerpt.locator:
Rain; begins “THE rain is raining all around,
It falls on field and tree,”; ends “It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.”.

questions.prompt: What two things receive rain in the second line?
facilitatorNotes: The field and tree are both named.
evidence: It falls on field and tree,

questions.prompt: Where does rain fall far from the umbrellas?
facilitatorNotes: It also falls on ships at sea, widening the scene.
evidence: And on the ships at sea.

questions.prompt: Which words do you hear again and again? What do they make the rain seem to do?
facilitatorNotes: Rain/raining/rains return through the short poem; they can suggest ongoing rain everywhere.
evidence: THE rain is raining all around,

days.title: Miss Moppet: a trick with a hole
days.challenge: Remember the hole before it changes the ending.
days.focus: A small object becomes the cause of a surprising escape.
days.context: Listen to a complete short animal story. A duster is a cleaning cloth; a bell-pull is a hanging cord that rings a bell.
days.contentNote: Comic animal chasing and rough handling: a kitten ties a mouse in a cloth, but he escapes unharmed. Do not imitate this treatment of animals.

excerpt.locator: The Story of Miss Moppet, complete; begins “This is a Pussy called Miss Moppet, she thinks she …” and ends “… is dancing a jig on the top of the cupboard!”.

questions.prompt: What happens when Moppet first jumps at the mouse?
facilitatorNotes: She misses the mouse and hits the cupboard. Ask the child to retell the two actions in order.
evidence: she misses the Mouse and hits her own head.

questions.prompt: How does the hole help Moppet first, and help the mouse later?
facilitatorNotes: Moppet peeks through it; later the mouse escapes through the cloth. Accept pointing to the two related moments.
evidence: looks at him through a hole in the duster.

questions.prompt: Does the storyteller approve when Moppet decides to tease the mouse? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says it is not nice. Invite discussion of both characters teasing without requiring a single moral.
evidence: which is not at all nice of Miss Moppet.

days.title: Seasons
days.challenge: Hold four seasonal pictures and notice the changed final attitude.
days.focus: Seasonal settings shift from outdoor wonder to winter warmth.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “SEASONS.”; opening “IN Spring-time, the Forest,”; ending “And Winter has glee.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 34, 35.

questions.prompt: Which place does the opening connect with spring? What new things grow there?
facilitatorNotes: The forest, with new buds, primrose and bluebell. Accept one named plant or bud detail.
evidence:
The primrose and bluebell
      Fresh-blown in the woods,

questions.prompt: What contrast does the winter verse make between daylight and firelight?
facilitatorNotes: Daylight is short while firelight is long. Discuss the feeling of a long cosy evening, without treating fire as something a child should handle.
evidence:
The daylight is short,
      But the firelight is long;

questions.prompt: The first winter line sighs “ah me!” How is winter described at the very end?
facilitatorNotes: Winter has glee. Skating, story and song help explain the more cheerful conclusion.
evidence: And Winter has glee.

days.title: Oh, fair to see
days.challenge: Compare two views of the same kind of tree.
days.focus: Parallel stanzas make blossom and fruit equally worth admiring.
days.context: “Laden” means loaded; “fair” here means beautiful. Listen for what fills each tree.

excerpt.locator:
Oh, fair to see; begins “Oh, fair to see
Bloom-laden cherry tree,”; ends “Oh, fair to see
Fruit-laden cherry tree,
With balls of shining red
Decking a leafy head,
Oh, fair to see!”.

questions.prompt: What color fills the tree in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The blossoms are imagined as sunny white clothing.
evidence: Arrayed in sunny white;

questions.prompt: What are the shining red balls in the second stanza?
facilitatorNotes: They are cherries, the fruit named at the beginning of that stanza.
evidence: Fruit-laden cherry tree,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker admire just the blossoms or both views?
facilitatorNotes: The same admiring words begin and end both stanzas.
evidence: Oh, fair to see!

days.title: The Bird
days.challenge: Follow repeated offers and refusals and infer the bird’s priorities.
days.focus: A bird prefers freedom and natural surroundings to luxurious gifts.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE BIRD.”; opening “"BIRDIE, Birdie, will you pet?”; ending “Good-bye, good-bye to my lady fair!"”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 41.

questions.prompt: Where would the bird rather sleep than in the offered velvet bed?
facilitatorNotes: In the ivy wall, where it hears rain without getting wet. Its own shelter is enough for it.
